headline_result_summary: In two randomized field experiments conducted with Nairobi's municipal water and sanitation utility across informal settlements where compounds had received subsidized/loan-financed piped water and sewer connections, systematic contract enforcement for nonpayment (targeted, transparent disconnection notices with hardship-exemption appeals and follow-through disconnection) had no statistically significant effect on any measure of household water or sanitation access, functionality, consumption, quality, or affordability nine months after implementation (piped water connection: -0.036, p = 0.135; working piped connection: -0.033, p = 0.423; pour-flush toilet: -0.014, p = 0.471; piped water as main source: +0.040, p = 0.286; metered consumption: +2.583, p = 0.901; monthly water expenditure: +$0.664, p = 0.509; weekly water-fetching time: -17.569 minutes, p = 0.418; tenant monthly rent: -$1.845, p = 0.474; owner and tenant service quality and fairness indices: all p >= 0.395). Although 96 of 327 targeted compounds were temporarily disconnected during enforcement, most were quickly reconnected upon agreeing to a payment plan, and public kiosks/vendors provided alternative water during interruptions. On utility financial outcomes (an indirect/non-access outcome), contract enforcement sharply increased property owner bill/loan payment likelihood (+30.0 percentage points at 1 month, p < 0.001; +19.5 percentage points at 9 months, p < 0.001) and total payments (+$8.78 at 1 month, p < 0.001; +$9.08 at 9 months, p = 0.031) with zero spillover effects, and landlords offset higher effective fee payments by renting out space on the extensive margin (+13.5 percentage points, p < 0.001) rather than raising tenant rents. A separate individually randomized face-to-face tenant engagement intervention designed to spur bottom-up accountability had a precisely estimated null effect on all payment outcomes (-0.005 at 1 month, p = 0.776; -0.002 at 9 months, p = 0.928).
specification_or_coding_pitfalls: 1. Confusing utility revenue collection with household water/sanitation access: The headline positive treatment effects in Table 5 (+0.300***, p < 0.001 on making a payment; +$8.783*** on amount paid) measure utility bill and connection-loan repayment by property owners—not household water or sanitation access. Every direct household access, functionality, consumption, water expenditure, fetching-time, satisfaction, and tenant rent outcome in Tables 7 and 8 is statistically null at 9 months. 2. Misinterpreting disconnection enforcement polarity or non-significant point estimates: Over-interpreting negative point estimates on piped connection (-0.036, p = 0.135) or working connection (-0.033, p = 0.423) as adverse access effects—or over-interpreting +0.040 (p = 0.286) on piped water as main source as favorable—would miscode noise. Contextual nuance: 96 of 327 assigned compounds experienced short-run disconnections in Nov-Dec 2018, but almost all were rapidly reconnected after agreeing to flexible payment plans. 3. Different control groups across tables: Administrative payment ITT regressions (Table 5, N = 1,001) compare treated compounds in treatment clusters (327) to disconnection-eligible compounds in pure control clusters (674) per Equation (2), whereas 9-month endline survey regressions (Tables 7 and 8, N = 334 to 608) compare treated compounds to untreated disconnection-eligible control compounds within enforcement-treatment clusters (322), because pure control clusters were not surveyed at endline (Table 6 Panel A shows no payment spillovers onto within-cluster controls). 4. Minor discrepancies between prose and tables: Section 8.5 (pp. 20-21) cites piped water as main source +4.4 pp (p = 0.243), monthly water spending $6.86 vs. $6.62 (p = 0.803), and fetching time 100 vs. 118 min (p = 0.388), whereas Table 7 prints +0.040 (p = 0.286), +0.664 (p = 0.509), and -17.569 (p = 0.418); likewise Table 7 prints tenant psychological well-being = 0.139 (SE 0.105) vs. Table A6 = 0.077 (SE 0.104). All remain statistically null. 5. Multiple-testing / borderline-p traps and non-experimental tables: In Appendix Table A1, owner perception that 'The water bills are accurate' is +0.113** (p = 0.014), which the authors discount due to multiple testing across 20+ sub-indicators (the overall fairness index is null, p = 0.404). In Table 8, landlord rent increase in last 6 months is borderline (+0.036*, p = 0.091) while tenant rent paid is null (-$1.845, p = 0.474). Finally, the 2014-2018 69% connection subsidy + loan expansion (90% take-up, 137,000 people) is non-experimental background (the planned top-up subsidy RCT was dropped, Appendix A.1), and Table 3 (N = 4,175) reports cross-sectional correlates where receiving water last week predicts bill payment rather than evaluating a governance exposure on access.
study_design: Two randomized controlled field experiments (RCTs): (1) an individually randomized trial of face-to-face tenant engagement stratified by informal settlement, and (2) a two-stage street-level cluster-randomized trial (stratified by settlement) of systematic contract enforcement via targeted, transparent disconnection notices and service disconnections for nonpayment, evaluated with administrative utility billing data (1 and 9 months post-intervention) and a 9-month endline survey of property owners and tenants (plus descriptive baseline OLS payment-correlate regressions).
unit_and_sample_size: Multi-household residential compounds (utility customer accounts held by property owners) and residing property owners / randomly selected tenant households across Nairobi informal settlements. Engagement RCT (administrative data, Table 4): N = 2,584 compounds with tenants across 6 settlements (1,292 treatment [885 reached], 1,292 control). Contract Enforcement RCT — administrative billing ITT (Table 5): N = 1,001 disconnection-eligible compounds across 142 street clusters in 4 settlements (327 assigned to treatment in 73 treatment clusters [299 notices delivered, 96 disconnected] vs. 674 eligible compounds in 74 pure control clusters; drawn from 3,253 accounts in 147 street clusters); spillover samples (Table 6): N = 996 eligible compounds (144 clusters) and N = 1,930 ineligible compounds (143 clusters). Contract Enforcement RCT — 9-month follow-up survey within enforcement-treatment clusters (Tables 7-8): N = 334 to 608 compounds/owners/tenants (e.g., N = 600 for piped water connection, N = 591 for working connection, N = 608 for pour-flush toilet and water satisfaction, N = 474 for meter reading, N = 334 for water expenditure, N = 357-403 for tenant outcomes, N = 364-568 for rental market outcomes). Observational payment correlates (Table 3): N = 4,164 to 4,175 compounds.
